title: Toxicity‐Weighted Pesticide Exposure in County‐Level Cancer Models: Endpoint Matching, Spatial Dependence, and Geographic Validation
content:
Abstract

The objective of this study was to evaluate whether toxicity-weighted pesticide exposure improves county-level cancer models, whether endpoint-matched metrics provide different model performance, and whether observed associations persist after accounting for spatial dependence and geographic validation. Data were collected for 3,107 U.S. counties, including USGS pesticide use estimates for 408 compounds during 2010–2012, cancer incidence from NCI and CDC State Cancer Profiles for 2018 to 2022, diabetes and coronary heart disease (CHD) prevalence from CDC PLACES, socioeconomic indicators from the U.S. Census, and climate variables from NOAA. Pesticide exposure was represented using applied mass, chronic reference dose (RfD) weighted load, cancer slope factor weighted load, and cancer weight of evidence. Model performance was assessed using adjusted R2, AIC, residual Moran's I, spatial error models, and leave-one-state-out cross validation. Although the RfD weighted load improved model fit for cancer incidence relative to applied mass (ΔAIC = −9.1), cancer-specific weighting did not provide a comparable improvement. The socioeconomic block produced the largest increase in model fit, while climate contributed to smaller improvements. Residual spatial autocorrelation remained strong after covariate adjustment, with Moran's I of 0.656 for the saturated cancer model. In the spatial error model, the coefficient for RfD weighted exposure decreased from β = 8.61 to β = 1.35 and was no longer statistically significant (p = 0.26). These findings show that toxicity weighting can change exposure priorities, but better model fit does not establish a toxicological or epidemiological relationship.
author: Naveen Joseph
